title: K-H-L
hook: kahal, kehillah: an assembly, a community

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-K-N: the mishkan, the Shechinah, and shachen, the neighbor. Your line was presence is neighborly. Whose name did you learn? Today, from the neighbor to the whole crowd. Day one thousand four hundred six.

There's a book in the Bible whose author doesn't give a name. Just a title. Kohelet. It opens with a man looking hard at life and calling all of it vapor, breath, here and gone. English Bibles call the book Ecclesiastes, and the speaker the Preacher. But Kohelet, in Hebrew, comes from a root that means to gather a crowd. Kohelet is something like the Gatherer, or the one who speaks to the assembly. A book this lonely-sounding is named for a crowd. Today's root is that crowd.
screen: `A BOOK WITH A TITLE, NOT A NAME.` → `KOHELET: THE GATHERER.` → `NAMED FOR A CROWD.`

segments.voice: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed. Kahal: an assembly, a congregation. Kehillah: a community. And the verb, to gather people together. Turn it three ways. First, the great gathering. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives an instruction for the festival of booths, once every seven years. Read the teaching aloud to everyone. And look who's on the list: "Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates." Not the leaders. Not the scholars. The whole crowd, with the kids and the newcomer, so that, the verse says, they may hear and learn. The rabbis called this gathering hakhel, from the same root: gather. Second, the community as a thing that lasts. Through the centuries, a Jewish town's organized community, with its synagogue, its burial society, its charity fund, its school, was called a kehillah. It's the word for the people who show up when there's a wedding, a shiva house, a bris, a sick neighbor. Some congregations still use it in their names today. Third, the warning. In the sayings of the fathers, Hillel teaches: don't separate yourself from the community. Hillel's word there is a different one, tzibbur, but the point lands on kehillah. You can learn alone. You can pray alone. But the tradition keeps pulling you back toward the room full of other people. Even Kohelet, sitting with his big questions, takes his name from the crowd he spoke them to.
screen: `KAHAL: THE ASSEMBLY.` · `GATHER MEN, WOMEN, CHILDREN, STRANGER.` · `KEHILLAH: THE COMMUNITY THAT SHOWS UP.` · `DON'T SEPARATE YOURSELF.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather people. Settle, and breathe. Think of the circles you belong to. Family. Friends. Coworkers. A team, a class, a street, a congregation. Let them come to mind as rooms full of faces. Now notice one circle that hasn't gathered in a while. The group chat that's gone quiet. The friends you keep meaning to see. Picture them in one room, at one table. Then think of one person who's usually left off the list, the newcomer, the stranger within your gates, and put them at the table too. If you pray, you can hold that circle in your prayer. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed: the root of kahal, the assembly; kehillah, the community; hakhel, the great gathering; and Kohelet, the Gatherer. Today's word.
Your line: community. Today, send the message that gets a few people in one place, even for a coffee, even on a call. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: Jewish communities are often called kehillot, and Jewish life gathers people for prayer, learning and the life cycle; some communities hold a hakhel gathering in the year after the sabbatical year, recalling Deuteronomy 31.

notes: Editor pass: replaced the fork and first myth, which repeated day 1403's Deuteronomy guest-list item; fork is now Hillel's 'don't separate yourself', myth items are Kohelet as a title and hakhel.
Kohelet glossed as 'the Gatherer' / 'the one who speaks to the assembly': standard explanation from K-H-L, but the exact sense is debated. Confirm phrasing.
Deuteronomy 31:10–12: 'at the end of every seven years ... in the feast of tabernacles' (31:10) supports 'once every seven years' at Sukkot; 31:12 quoted from KJV. Confirm.
The term hakhel for this gathering is from the root used in 31:12 and is the rabbinic name (Mishnah Sotah 7:8). Confirm.
Kehillah as the organized community of a Jewish town (with burial society, charity, school): stated generally without dates. 'Some congregations still use it in their names' is general usage.
Pirkei Avot 2:4 (2:5 in some editions): Hillel, al tifrosh min hatzibbur, paraphrased; the script notes the word there is tzibbur.
